doc.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Gene Lees, Jazz Letter and the Goodman Russian tour essay
summary: Gene Lees invites an article on the Goodman Russian tour, which grows into a long essay and leads Oxford to approach him.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: material. I’ve been doing it for something like twelve years now. And I still every time I put together my month’s column I look and I see that I still have enough for another column in my computer, and by the time I get around to the next month I’ve gathered enough other things that I’ve still, I’ve never had to reach back or hurry and interview somebody. It’s just been a natural thing. So well I really got started writing again in the 80s there someplace. I knew Gene Lees who had been the editor of Down Beat for quite a while, in one of his past lives, and during that period I’d gotten to know him because he was hanging around Jim & Andy’s in New York a lot and he got to know a lot of the musicians. And he was also a songwriter. And he had ended up out in California and was publishing a little, like a monthly newsletter called “Jazz Letter.” And I can’t remember, because he’d been doing this for a couple of years before I’d heard about it, somebody sent me a gift subscription I guess it was. And I was so pleased with it that, you know the stuff that he wrote and stuff that other people wrote that he would put in there, so I wrote him a letter and said do you have any back issues available, and he sends me a gift of all of the back issues for the last two years, and also a letter that said I remember when you came back from the Russian tour with Benny Goodman in the 60s there, that you told a lot of funny stories about what a catastrophe that trip was, and what would you think about doing an article for “Jazz Letter” you know. He says I can’t pay you anything but you can tell it the way it was and I promise not to edit it. So I got to thinking about it and thought it would be fun to do, and I figured when I started it would just be recollections, I could do it in maybe 2,000 words and that would be that. But as I started getting back into it, then I started calling up guys that were on the band that were still around — Phil Woods and Jerry Dodgion and different guys. Joe Wilder — I was working with Joe Wilder at that time, and Wayne Andre and Jimmy Maxwell. And so we reconstructed the thing and I got more and more material, and it ended up being quite a long essay. Gene published it in about four different issues of “Jazz Letter.” And that got me back into the business of not just writing but of trying to write well, which for me means writing it down and then going back and editing it about four hundred times until you get it said, you know get the sentences to really say what you want them to say and get the ambiguities out of there and try to get the organization of the thing so that it goes somewhere. And when it was all over, I was still doing the column and stuff life that, and I guess Sheldon Meyer, one of the heads of the New York Oxford University Press Division is a jazz fan, and had been instrumental in getting a number of autobiographies published there. And Gene was one of his writers, and Dick Sudhalter was one of his writers. So when he asked these, I guess Oxford had done some other anecdote collections, one from the theater, one from literature, one from the opera, one from the military or something like that.
